title: The Village That Owned a Factory

pages.text: At a village near Nsawam, farmers gathered beside a mountain of pineapples. Some fruits were beginning to spoil. ‘The buyers offered us too little,’ complained Mr. Boateng. ‘If we wait much longer, we may lose the harvest,’ said another farmer. Fourteen-year-old Naa watched her mother count the unsold fruit. ‘Why don’t we make pineapple juice ourselves?’ she asked. Her mother sighed. ‘That requires equipment, suitable premises, food-safety controls, workers and money.’ Naa looked at the farmers. ‘But there are so many of us. What if we worked together?’

pages.alt: Pineapple farmers near Nsawam gathered beside a large pile of harvested pineapples while fourteen-year-old Naa speaks with her mother and Mr. Boateng.

pages.text: That evening, Naa drew a picture of a small processing factory. Her friend Sadiq helped her prepare a presentation. They visited the local farmers’ association with their teacher. ‘We are not suggesting that children should operate a factory,’ Naa began. ‘We are asking whether adults could investigate a business that processes some of the fruit locally.’ The farmers listened. One woman raised her hand. ‘Who would own this business?’ Naa smiled. ‘Perhaps the members could own it together.’

pages.text: An experienced cooperative adviser visited the community. ‘A cooperative is an organisation owned and controlled by its members for their shared benefit,’ she explained. ‘Its rules determine membership, voting, contributions and how any surplus is used.’ ‘Does everyone automatically earn money?’ Sadiq asked. ‘No. A cooperative can make losses, just like other businesses.’ The adviser explained that the farmers needed a feasibility study, a suitable legal structure, proper records and clear governance. ‘Working together is powerful,’ she said, ‘but good intentions cannot replace sound management.’

pages.text: The farmers prepared a simplified classroom budget for a proposed pilot project. In the illustrative pilot budget, equipment was GH₵40,000, facility improvements were GH₵20,000, and initial supplies and working capital were GH₵20,000, giving a total required of GH₵80,000. ‘If forty members each contribute GH₵1,000, how much will they raise?’ the adviser asked. Naa calculated quickly. ‘GH₵40,000!’ ‘Correct. They would still need GH₵40,000.’ ‘Could they borrow it?’ Sadiq asked. ‘Possibly, if suitable financing is available and affordable. But borrowing creates repayment obligations. They must assess the risks first.’

pages.text: At school, their teacher explained two ways businesses and other eligible issuers may raise funds. ‘When investors buy shares in a company, they acquire an ownership interest. When investors buy bonds, they generally lend money to the issuer under specified terms.’ ‘Do shareholders always receive dividends?’ Naa asked. ‘No. Dividends are not guaranteed.’ ‘Are bonds always safe?’ ‘No. Issuers can fail to pay, and bond values can change.’ Naa wrote: Shares = ownership. Bonds = lending. Both involve risk. Their teacher reminded them that a cooperative’s member contributions and ownership rules may differ from ordinary company shares.

pages.text: After several months of professional advice and planning, the adults organised a small, properly supervised processing trial using suitable licensed facilities. The first batch of juice tasted wonderful. But the packaging cost more than expected. Transport was expensive too. ‘Then our profit is smaller than we hoped,’ said the cooperative treasurer. Naa looked disappointed. Her mother smiled. ‘That is why we test ideas before expanding. A successful trial must include accurate costs, safe production and real customer demand.’

pages.text: At a members’ meeting, the treasurer presented the accounts. ‘These are our sales, expenses, outstanding bills and cash balance.’ One member suggested hiding some costs to make the business look more attractive. The chairperson refused. ‘Investors, lenders and members deserve accurate information.’ The cooperative arranged appropriate independent financial oversight and agreed to report regularly to members. Naa whispered to Sadiq, ‘Good governance is part of business success.’

pages.text: Over time, the cooperative improved its operations and won regular orders. It hired workers for production, quality assurance, logistics and administration. The farmers continued monitoring costs, food safety and market demand. One afternoon, Naa met a young employee who had recently completed vocational training. ‘This job helps me support my family,’ he told her. Naa felt proud. The business was not simply selling juice. It was creating opportunities.

pages.text: At the cooperative’s anniversary meeting, Naa stood beside her mother. ‘Did you ever imagine this?’ she asked. ‘I imagined earning a fair return for our fruit,’ her mother said. ‘But I did not know where the journey would lead.’ Naa looked at the workers and farmers. ‘One idea brought people together. Knowledge helped them plan. Investment provided resources. Good management helped them continue.’ Her mother nodded. ‘And everyone still has to work hard to keep the business healthy.’ Naa opened a fresh notebook. On the first page, she wrote: What other problems can we solve together?

activities.question: What is one important feature of a cooperative?
options: It is owned and controlled by its members under agreed rules.
It is guaranteed by law never to make a loss.
Only one person makes every decision without rules.
activities.explanation: A cooperative is owned and controlled by its members for their shared benefit under agreed rules.

activities.question: Forty members contribute GH₵1,000 each. How much is raised?
Required capital is GH₵80,000 and members raise GH₵40,000. What remains?
activities.explanation: GH₵80,000 required - GH₵40,000 raised = GH₵40,000 remaining.

activities.question: What does owning shares in a company generally mean?
options: Owning an interest in a company
Lending money with a guaranteed fixed payment
Receiving a guaranteed dividend every month
activities.explanation: When investors buy shares in a company, they acquire an ownership interest.

activities.question: What does buying a bond generally mean?
options: Lending to an issuer under specified terms
Becoming the sole owner of a cooperative farm
Eliminating all financial risk
activities.explanation: When investors buy bonds, they generally lend money to the issuer under specified terms.

activities.question: Can a cooperative make losses?
options: Yes, a cooperative can make losses just like other businesses.
No, cooperatives automatically earn profits every year.
No, packaging and transport never cost money.
activities.explanation: Yes. A cooperative can make losses, just like other businesses, which is why sound management and feasibility testing matter.

activities.question: Why should the treasurer report all expenses honestly?
options: To support transparency, accountability and informed decisions
To hide packaging costs from the members
So members do not know the cash balance
activities.explanation: Accurate reporting supports transparency, accountability and informed decisions for members, lenders and investors.

activities.definition: An organisation owned and controlled by its members for their shared benefit under agreed rules
distractors: A business where expenses are hidden from the members
A scheme that guarantees nobody can ever make a loss

activities.prompt: Order the stages of how the pineapple cooperative was planned and built.
items: Naa and Sadiq ask if farmers can form a pineapple cooperative.
An adviser explains cooperative rules and the GH₵80,000 budget.
Adults run a licensed trial and report all expenses honestly.
The cooperative improves operations and creates local jobs.

activities.prompt: How did Naa feel when she met the young vocational graduate whose new job at the cooperative helped him support his family?

glossary.definition: An organisation owned and controlled by its members for their shared benefit under agreed rules.
An assessment of whether a proposed project or business plan is practical and financially viable.
The system of rules, oversight and accountability used to direct and manage an organisation.
Units of ownership interest in a company.
Debt instruments where an investor lends money to an issuer under specified terms.
Payments made by a company to its shareholders out of profits (not guaranteed).
The careful organisation of storing, handling and transporting goods to customers.
